results.ground_truth_answer:
Welcome to a great game! PFC Schussel is not an example of an infantry gun. For the Germans, the infantry guns are personality cards 28 and 29, the 37mm and 50mm antitank guns. I think my rules are the original edition, and my 8.52 says “medium machine gun, mortar, or Infantry Gun may not fire from a Stream… Other crewed weapons may fire from a Stream only if they are fully crewed and non-moving, and even then must use their bracketed Firepower or To Hit frequency.” Schussel and his LMG can fire from the stream if he has an assigned crewman helping him and the group is not moving. I want to make sure I get this right (42.6 and 42.7): 

VARIANT A) Prolonging the game after victory by voluntary withdrawal

Exception: At some point a squad break or fullfillment of victory condition might happen, in which case Variant B kicks in and overrides variant A (the game will then be more likely to end). 

42.72 does not use the words "ends immediately" in its text.  What is variant A and Variant B?  What are you talking about?

3. The opponent can pursue and prevent the withdrawal of a group by keeping/moving one of his groups to RR5 to a withdrawing group AND passing a morale check with his unpinned SL (the SL can be anywhere on the board, he doesn't need to be part of the "pursuing" group). The morale check does not count as an action for the SL's group - it's free. 

4. A group trying to withdraw will keep trying automatically every turn? Thus, the pursuing player needs to keep his group at RR5 and his SL needs to pass a morale check every single turn in order to prolong the game?

VARIANT B) Prolonging the game after victory by squad break or scenario victory conditions

1. Once he has fulfilled the scenario's victory condition or has broken the opponent's squad, the victorious player can try to prolong the game by passing a morale check with his unpinned squad leader. The morale check does not count as an action for the SL's group - it's free. If the check succeeds, another round is played (and the SL may test again for another round, etc). If the check fails, the game ends. 

I will just explain the rule:

Basically a scenario in a Campaign game can end in 4 ways:
-  Voluntary withdrawl and concession  by one side per 42.6.
-  Squad break
-  Victory conditions.
-  End of final deck.

On the winning player's winning turn or turn following his opponent's announcement of a withdrawl of a group, the winning player may declare a pursuit, if there are cards left in the deck-so no pursuits if won by time limit.  His active SL (including ASL promoted to SL due SL elimination per errata) must pass a morale check to initiate pursuit (Failure = no pursuit will be attempted.)  This is done once during the game.  Often a winning player will reject pursuit if the potential additional casualties wouldn't be worth the additional advantages (usually just a few elan points).  If the pursuit was not initiated, either voluntarily or failure of the morale check, the game end immediately at the end of the winning player's turn.

If a group attempts withdrawl, it succeeds on the next turn unless the opponent both initiates pursuit (or had initiated pursuit previously) and has a group @ RR5 to the withdrawing group. Since the withdrawing group is in the act of retrograde movement (i.e. retreating to a negative range chit), the pursuing group must usually move forward to be at RR5.  If at the end of the next turn, if pursuit was not declared or no persuing enemy groups are at RR5, the withdrawing group is removed from play--it succeded in its withdrawal. A group that is encircled cannot attempt withdrawal.

Once a pursuit is declared, the game now ends with if all opposing groups are withdrawn (or eliminated) OR the end of the next deck.  (This is why you can't pursue when win on time limit.)

results.ground_truth_answer:

Since the movement card on a group which has forded a stream must be in sideways mode, if it rejects terrain, it has to remove the movement card, and would have to ford the stream again in order to move.

The British survivors moved forward again (to RR2) in their next play, and the Japanese Banzai group moved backwards (to RR3) to keep the range at RR5, and again went into CC immediately, finally killing the rest of the British group C for the win. Again, I think we screwed up by allowing the Japanese to play a movement card to change the range to RR5 AND go into CC in the same turn. As long as the British run away, the Japanese can chase them, but not fight them in CC in the same move. Just looking for confirmation before discussing this again with my opponent, because he was sure we were doing it right. Is my interpretation of 45.422 correct?

Main question: In the rules (45.43), it says that "The Japanese player has the option to cancel a Banzai attack only if the target group retreats or moves away laterally out of range (i.e. the target group is no longer directly opposite or adjacent), or if another enemy group moves in such a way as to block the access of the Banzai group to the declared target." Give GeekGold Tip

If the defending group moves away, the Banzaiing group could move this turn to get back to RR5 and then enter Cc on the following turn.

If it were crewed, then its malf is X6 and therefore it only ***potentially*** breaks on a Red 6.  (Because the RPC would include all firing weapons, crewman, malfed weapon specified in the rules.) That's  the risk of firing when it is not fully crewed.

I'll start by saying "You're  welcome", to the many thanks given above.

Malfunction is one the areas of the ruled where so many ideas were included, that that when any question comes up, you can't really point to any one place in the rules.  One question leads to another...... The original errata keeper, Andy Maly, couldn't either.  Basically, my answer above is the whole errata.

I could see what AH was trying to do with malfunction rules.  They wanted different weapons (particularly uncrewed MGs) to have different rates of failure. They wanted the resolution of the attack to be have a lower effect on the remaining men in target group, but they wanted a single weapon that broke to fall silent.  They wanted FTs & captured weapons  to be very prone to failure.  They wanted the possibility of broken weapons to be permanently broken.  They wanted MG belts to temporarily jam. Then they listed each of these ideas as individual rules instead of coming up with a process to determine which rule applies when (which the errata ends up doing)

Could the malfunction rules have been made simpler?  Sure!  They could have made the malfunction occur after the completion of fire attack resolution.  (But that would remove the tactical play order of men in the group--the ones at the end of line have slightly lower fire attacks than the front of the line. And to add to that, from a realism point of view, there are still major issues:
A) The more men in the firing group, the less chance each weapon will break.  (When there are 3 men in the firing group, when a malfunction occurs, 1/3 chance that weapon A breaks.  5 firing men, 1/5 chance weapon A breaks.)
B)  The more men in target group, the greater the chance a weapon breaks.  (Firing at 3 men, 3 chances that the dreaded Red 6 will come up.  5 men, 5 chances.)

But for fixing those issues, the cure would be far worse than the disease.  DO NOT GO THERE!

-  All FP at the encircled group is doubled from any group (not just from the flanked group.)
- The encircled group cannot  receive or exit individual transferring men.  Or laterally transfer to change its group ID.
-  Panic -1.

To get out of an encirclement requires either:
- elimination of either group forming the encircle (including if either group moved away via lateral transfer.
- the encircled group infiltrates either encircling group, 
- either encircling group is RR1 or further from the encircled group, or
- if both encircling groups end up in front of the encircled group. ie.  The encircled group retreated to get away in these last two situations.)
